description.current: The Wairarapa lies just over the Remutaka Range from Wellington and is known for its wineries, especially around Martinborough. Towns such as Greytown and Masterton have historic main streets, cafés and boutiques. The south coast has Cape Palliser's lighthouse, seal colonies and the Putangirua Pinnacles.
description.proposed: The Wairarapa is the south-eastern corner of the North Island, separated from the Wellington area by the Remutaka Range and popular with Wellington day-trippers. The Remutaka and Tararua ranges shelter it from the prevailing westerlies, giving a warm, dry climate, and wine centres on Martinborough, where pinot noir and sauvignon blanc are the two main varieties. Masterton is the largest town, with Carterton, Greytown and Featherston strung along the way. More than 1,000 people commute 'through the hill' to Wellington each day.
variants: The Wairarapa is the south-eastern corner of the North Island, separated from the Wellington area by the Remutaka Range and popular with Wellington day-trippers. The Remutaka and Tararua ranges shelter it from the prevailing westerlies, giving a warm, dry climate, and wine centres on Martinborough, where pinot noir and sauvignon blanc are the two main varieties. Masterton is the largest town, with Carterton, Greytown and Featherston strung along the way. More than 1,000 people commute 'through the hill' to Wellington each day.

Sheltered from the prevailing westerlies by the Remutaka and Tararua ranges, the Wairarapa has a warm, dry climate that suits grapes, and the main wine area is around Martinborough. Masterton is the largest town, with Carterton, Greytown and Featherston to its south. Beyond them the land runs out to a rugged south coast, while to the north Pūkaha keeps kiwi and takahē in a forest sanctuary on State Highway 2.

Over the Remutaka Range from Wellington, the Wairarapa is a warm, dry region of vineyards and small towns, with Masterton the largest. Pinot noir and sauvignon blanc are the two main wine varieties, grown mostly around Martinborough. Trains run to Masterton, and the forested Tararua Range rises behind the plain.
description.reason: Cut the unsourced 'historic main streets, cafés and boutiques' (none of the loaded sources describes them for Greytown or Masterton). Facts from Wikivoyage Wairarapa (towns, shelter, climate, pinot noir and sauvignon blanc, wine centred on Martinborough) and Wikipedia (day-trippers/commuters). Cape Palliser and the Pinnacles are dropped from the description because they now appear in the reasons and spot bios (no repetition). Variant 2 uses Pūkaha for the north; variant 3 is three sentences.

current.title: Day-trip from Wellington
current.detail: The Wairarapa Line runs trains to Masterton, and Martinborough is about 90 minutes by road.

current.title: Book a designated driver
current.detail: Wineries are close together in Martinborough, and cycling or a tour avoids drinking and driving.

current.title: Keep your distance from seals
current.detail: Fur seals at Cape Palliser can be aggressive if approached, so stay at least 10 metres away.

proposed.title: Trains stop at Masterton
proposed.detail: The Wairarapa Line runs 91 km from Wellington to Masterton, with five services each way Monday to Friday but only two at weekends and on public holidays. There is no train to Martinborough; Metlink bus 200 runs there from Masterton and Featherston.

proposed.title: Hire a bike, not a car
proposed.detail: Martinborough's vineyards lie in ribbons around the north and east of town, and the Martinborough Wine Centre hires cycles, which avoids drinking and driving.

proposed.title: Give seals 20 metres
proposed.detail: DOC advises staying at least 20 metres from fur seals, which have sharp teeth and move quickly if threatened. Keep dogs leashed and away, and never get between a seal and the sea.

standaloneSpots.name: Tararua Forest Park

bio.current: A large forest park of ridges and tramping tracks above the Kāpiti and Wairarapa plains, managed by the Department of Conservation.
bio.proposed: New Zealand's first forest park, established in 1954, 1,150 square kilometres of Tararua Range bush, huts and tracks that rise to 1,571 m at Mitre, entered from Holdsworth, Waiohine Gorge or Ōtaki Forks.
variants: New Zealand's first forest park, established in 1954, 1,150 square kilometres of Tararua Range bush, huts and tracks that rise to 1,571 m at Mitre, entered from Holdsworth, Waiohine Gorge or Ōtaki Forks.
A range of ridges and open tops where cold southerlies have caused several fatalities, so routes across the tops are for experienced trampers only.
Tararua tramping, hunting and walking country covering 1,150 square kilometres between the Kāpiti Coast and the Wairarapa.
bio.reason: Supported in substance, but the first-forest-park fact (Wikipedia) and the three DOC entrances make it distinctive. Holdsworth detail stays in wairarapa-7 and the crossing in the Southern Crossing bio, so there is no repetition.

standaloneSpots.name: Remutaka Forest Park

bio.current: A forest park on the Remutaka Range between the Hutt Valley and Wairarapa, with tracks, rivers and the Catchpool Valley.
bio.proposed: A 22,000-hectare forest park across the Remutaka Range, with a campground and swimming spots in the Catchpool Valley 30 km from Wellington and kiwi released since 2006.
variants: A 22,000-hectare forest park across the Remutaka Range, with a campground and swimming spots in the Catchpool Valley 30 km from Wellington and kiwi released since 2006.
A tramping and hunting park with six bookable huts, where the Catchpool Valley leads to longer tramps in the Ōrongorongo Valley.
A forest park with Wairarapa-side entries along Western Lake Road at Waiorongomai, Battery Stream and Ocean Beach.
bio.reason: The stored bio's 'tracks, rivers' is generic. DOC and Wikipedia supply the area, Catchpool Valley campground and swimming, huts, Ōrongorongo tramps, Western Lake Road entries and 2006 kiwi release. The Rail Trail start at Cross Creek is left to the Rimutaka Incline spot so the two do not repeat each other.

standaloneSpots.name: Tararua Southern Crossing

bio.current: A classic two-day tramp across the exposed main range of the Tararuas between Ōtaki Forks and Mount Holdsworth.
bio.proposed: A 32 km alpine tramp of two to three days from Ōtaki Forks over Mount Hector to Kaitoke, one of the Tararua Range's four classic tramps and for experienced trampers only.
variants: A 32 km alpine tramp of two to three days from Ōtaki Forks over Mount Hector to Kaitoke, one of the Tararua Range's four classic tramps and for experienced trampers only.
DOC's advanced three-day route over Mount Hector (1,529 m) with Field, Kime and Alpha huts, notorious for strong winds, mist and freezing temperatures.
A route from Ōtaki Forks to Kaitoke across the exposed tops, popularised in the 1920s and 1930s by the Tararua Tramping Club.
bio.reason: Stored bio is wrong on two counts: the crossing ends at Kaitoke, not Mount Holdsworth (Ōtaki Forks to Holdsworth is the separate Middle Crossing, four days), and it takes three days (DOC) or two to three (Wikipedia), not two. 'Experienced trampers only' and wind/mist follow DOC. Tramping-club history is DOC.

hours.reason: 'Hut booking required' is not sourced: DOC lists the huts as Standard category and the loaded page does not say bookings are required. Hut fees are not loaded.

visitHoursMin/Max.reason: DOC leg times add to 19-23 hours of walking: Ōtaki Forks to Field Hut 3-4 h, Field to Kime 3-4 h, Kime to Alpha 5-6 h, Alpha to Kaitoke 8-9 h, over three days. Elapsed time with weather will be longer.
